title: WFS 452
text:
Welcome!
This book was built to host the working materials for WFS 452: Analysis and Interpretation of Fisheries Data. We will learn fisheries vocabulary, work through applied examples in R, keep track of our thinking in Quarto, and practice interpreting data the way fisheries managers actually use it.

title: WFS 452
text:
COURSE LOGISTICS

Catalog description
This course covers theory and application of sample design, analysis, and interpretation of freshwater fisheries data. Topics include fisheries management study design, recruitment, mortality, age and growth, abundance, biomass and production, size structure, bioenergetics, and development of management plans.


Student learning outcomes
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

calculate and interpret fish population metrics commonly used in fisheries management
define and use standard fisheries vocabulary, abbreviations, notation, and equations
read, summarize, and discuss journal papers in fisheries ecology and management
apply course tools to real-world management and conservation case studies



Software expectations
We will use Excel, R, and RStudio. Please do not plan on using Google Sheets for course calculations.


Grading

Assignments: 25%
Exams (2): 30% total

Take-home exam: 10%
In-class exam: 20%

Final project: 20%
Flipped classroom: 20%
Participation: 5%



Participation and AI use
This is a flipped course. If you are disengaged during team-led and in-class work, your participation score will drop.
You may use generative AI tools to help you study, outline, or debug. However, submitted work must be in your own words, reflect your own reasoning, and include a brief note acknowledging meaningful AI assistance.

title: 3  Sampling
text:
4.1 Random sampling
You are working in a small pond in New England. This pond has exactly 100 American eels (Anguila rostrata). The mean total length of this population is 100-cm. Similar to the example we did in class, we will be randomly sampling a small number (n=12) and estimating the mean of the population. We will also be estimating the standard error. In this case, we know the real population mean (100-cm) and thus, we can tell whether our mean estimate was close or not to the real population mean!



American Eel


We will be doing this pretty straightforward exercise in both Excel and program R.
On Canvas there should be 2 files. Download both of them. Use eel.xlsx for excel, and eel.csv for program R.

4.1.1 Excel
When you download and open the file you should see the following:

This file contains the size of EVERY SINGLE INDIVIDUAL in the population (100 eels). We will be sampling 15 individuals at random.
Before we do that, you should make sure I am not lying to you and check whether the mean length is actually 100.
In cell B102 you can estimate the mean population length by typing:
=AVERAGE(B2:B101)
If you get 100, you can continue, if you don’t, figure out what’s going on before continuing.

4.1.1.1 Let’s sample!
Let’s now assume we are out fishing and you catch 12 individuals (random sampling). Selecting a random sample in excel is annoying, but we will do it once. Moving forward, we will be using R.
In order to create a random sample, name column C “sample Length” and then we can sample our 12 individuals. Unfortunately, Excel does not have a great function for sampling without replacement… so, we need to add the Data analysis add-in:
In order to add data analysis go to File > Options > Add-Ins, then in the “Manage” dropdown, select “Excel Add-ins” and click “Go”. In the available add-ins list, check the box next to “Data Analysis Add-in” and click “OK”.
Now, with this data analysis add-in we can sample. Go to “Data”, and on the Analyze section you should be able to see the Analysis Add-in. Click it and select “sampling”.
For input range select ALL the lengths from the individuals (all 100). For number of samples select 12, and select C2:C13 as the output range.


4.1.1.2 Estimates
Next, estimate the mean of your sample using the AVERAGE function. Estimate the Standard Deviation using STDEV.S and a confidence interval using CONFIDENCE.T with an alpha of 0.05. If you don’t know how to do it check this 🔗 website 🔗.
You can also raise your hand if you’re still having issues.



4.1.2 Program R

4.1.2.1 Reminders for those new to R
You can skip this section if you feel comfortable with R
When using RStudio, you should avoid writing code in the “console”. Remember this screen?

Open R-Studio and make sure you are on your WFS452 project. Go to file > new script. If you only see three screens, make sure to press the button in the red square, and then you should look something like this:

Write all your code in the source section. Then you can run each line by pressing the run button or by hitting ctrl + enter.
You can import data of various formats into R; they include data tables in the form of .dbf, .csv, and .xlsx files or even spatial data such as vectors .shp or rasters .nc.
But the most common type of data files imported into R are probably.csv files.
You can import the dataset using the function read.csv()

How do you find the file path?
For mac, open Finder, click to the folder where you saved your data, find your file, right-click (or ctrl-click) it, and then click on GetInfo.
For Windows, you can search documents, or you can look at the latest downloads on your browser.
When we read a datafile, we need to create an “R object”. We can do it this way:
\[
\underbrace{eel}_{Object\; name} \; \; \; \underbrace{<-}_{arrow} \; \; \underbrace{read.csv('eel.csv')}_{Data}
\]



4.1.3 R questions
If you skipped the previous section, continue here
If you want to look at the top five rows of your head you can use the following:

We will do the same exact analysis we did in excel. First, we need to confirm the population mean:

And do a histogram of the population using hist(). If you need help with a function, you can run ?hist to open the help file.






Question 1

Then, let’s sample 12 individuals using:

And now estimate the mean using mean(). Call this object mean.eels, then print it by using mean.eels. You should do all this in the same chunk (sample, mean, and print).
Be aware than your sample will be different than your excel sample.






Question 2



2.1 In Quarto, as text, not in a chunk, write down the estimated mean from the previous code.
2.2 Run that same line again (sample, mean and print). You can do this by pressing the green play button that is on the chunk. Write the new mean in your quarto file, again as text, not in a chunk.
2.3 Do 1.2 10 times. Write all the means. Describe how close or far they are


For your last value, estimate the mean, the standard deviation using sd, and the confidence interval using the following equation:
\[
CI = mean \pm CritValue*std.err
\]
To obtain the critical value, you use:

crit<-qt(0.975,df=12-1) #trust me on this for now

And to estimate the standard error you use:
\[
std.err = st.dev \div  \sqrt{n}
\]
And remember that n is 12.
Now, lets do a fun simulation.
First off, let’s install a package.
YOU ONLY NEED TO INSTALL A PACKAGE ONCE, AND YOU SHOULD NOT DO IN A QUARTO FILE. COPY THIS AND RUN IT IN THE CONSOLE:

install.packages("ggplot2")

That is a package that will help us make some nice plots. ow that you installed itm you do not have to install it ever again in your computer.
On you Quarto file, copy and run the following code, it may seem complex, it is OK if you do not fully understand it.

set.seed(123)
mu=mean(eel$Length)
experiment<-1:100
n<-12
means<-rep(NA,100) #For the means
s<-rep(NA,100) #sd
SE<-rep(NA,100) #SE
LCI<-rep(NA,100) # Lower CI
UCI<-rep(NA,100) # Upper CI
inclusive<-rep(NA,100) #is the real parameter included?
alpha<-0.05 #our alpha
lower<-qnorm(alpha/2) #lower critical value
upper<-qnorm(1-alpha/2) #upper critical value
for(i in 1:100){
sample<-sample(eel$Length,n)
means[i]<-mean(sample)
s[i]<-sd(sample)
SE[i]<-s[i]/sqrt(n)
LCI[i]<-means[i]+SE[i]*lower
UCI[i]<-means[i]+SE[i]*upper
if(mu<UCI[i] & mu> LCI[i]){
  inclusive[i]<-T} else{
    inclusive[i]<-F
  }
}

df<-data.frame(experiment,means,s,SE,LCI,UCI,inclusive)


library(ggplot2)


ggplot(df, aes(x = experiment, y = means,colour=inclusive,ymin = LCI, ymax=UCI)) +
   geom_point() +
   geom_hline(yintercept = mu, color = "black", linetype = "longdash") +
   scale_y_continuous(name = "", limits = c(min(df$LCI) - min(df$LCI)/10 , max(df$UCI + max(df$UCI)/10))) +
   scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
   theme_classic()+
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#ec280e", "#06b512"))+
  labs(x= "sampling event", y="estimate")+
  geom_errorbar(width = 0)

title: 4  Age-Length Keys & Von Bertalanffy Growth
text:
5.1 Background
When fisheries biologists sample a fish population, they can easily measure the length of every fish they catch. However, determining the age of a fish (by reading otoliths, scales, or other hard structures) is time-consuming and expensive. Because of this, biologists typically age only a subsample of the fish they catch.
So how do we figure out the age composition of the entire catch? We use an Age-Length Key (ALK)!
An ALK uses the aged subsample to estimate the probability that a fish of a given length belongs to a certain age class. We then apply those probabilities to the unaged fish to assign ages to the full sample.



Redear Sunfish otolith cross-section showing annuli (growth rings)


Today we will:

Load a real dataset with age and length data
Build an Age-Length Key
Visualize the ALK with a bubble plot and an area plot
Fit a Von Bertalanffy growth curve to the age-length data.

text:
5.4 Part 3: Simulating a Field Scenario
In real life, we would measure the length of ALL fish but only age a smaller subsample. Let’s simulate that.
We already know how many fish we have.
Now, let’s create length categories (also called length bins). This groups fish into intervals. We will use 10-mm length bins:

CreekChub$LenCat <- lencat(CreekChub$len, w = 10)

Let’s look at what happened:

head(CreekChub)

Notice a new column LenCat was added. Each fish is now assigned to a length bin.
Now, let’s simulate our field scenario. We will randomly sample some fish to “age” (our aged subsample), and the rest will be “unaged”:

set.seed(452) # So everyone gets the same result

# Randomly select ~40% of fish to be "aged"
n <- nrow(CreekChub)
aged_indices <- sample(1:n, size = round(0.45 * n))

# Create aged and unaged datasets
aged <- CreekChub[aged_indices, ]
unaged <- CreekChub[-aged_indices, ]







Question 2 (1 pt)

title: 4  Age-Length Keys & Von Bertalanffy Growth
text:
5.5 Part 4: Building the Age-Length Key
Now, let’s build the Age-Length Key from our aged subsample. The ALK tells us: for a fish in a given length category, what is the probability it belongs to each age class?

raw <- xtabs(~ LenCat + age, data = aged)
raw

This gives us the raw counts - how many aged fish in each length bin belong to each age. Now let’s convert those to proportions (probabilities):

alk <- prop.table(raw, margin = 1)
round(alk, 2)

The margin = 1 means we calculate proportions across each row (each length category). Each row should sum to 1.






Question 3 (1 pt)

title: 4  Age-Length Keys & Von Bertalanffy Growth
text:
5.6 Part 5: Bubble Plot
A bubble plot is a great way to visualize an ALK. The size of each bubble represents the proportion of fish at that age within each length category.

# Convert ALK to a data frame for plotting
alk_df <- as.data.frame(alk)
colnames(alk_df) <- c("LenCat", "Age", "Proportion")
alk_df$LenCat <- as.numeric(as.character(alk_df$LenCat))
alk_df$Age <- as.numeric(as.character(alk_df$Age))

# Remove zero proportions for cleaner plotting
alk_df <- alk_df[alk_df$Proportion > 0, ]

ggplot(alk_df, aes(x = Age, y = LenCat, size = Proportion)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Length Category (mm)",
       title = "Age-Length Key: Bubble Plot") +
  theme_classic()







Question 4 (1 pt)



Describe the pattern you see in the bubble plot. Is there a general trend between age and length? Are there any length categories where fish could be multiple ages?

An area plot (also called a stacked area chart) shows the same information differently. It displays how the age composition changes across length categories.

colnames(alk_df2) <- c("LenCat", "Age", "Proportion")
alk_df2$LenCat <- as.numeric(as.character(alk_df2$LenCat))
alk_df2$Age <- factor(alk_df2$Age)

ggplot(alk_df2, aes(x = LenCat, y = Proportion, fill = Age)) +
  geom_area(position = "stack", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Length Category (mm)", y = "Proportion",
       title = "Age-Length Key: Area Plot",
       fill = "Age") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3") +

title: 4  Age-Length Keys & Von Bertalanffy Growth
text:
5.9 Part 8: Von Bertalanffy Growth Curve
Now that we have age-length data for the full sample, let’s fit a Von Bertalanffy growth curve.
Remember the equation:
\[
L_t = L_\infty (1-e^{-K(t-t_0)})
\]
Where:

\(L_t\) = expected length at age \(t\)
\(L_\infty\) = asymptotic maximum length
\(K\) = Brody growth coefficient (how fast fish approach \(L_\infty\))
\(t_0\) = theoretical age at length zero

First, let’s plot the raw age-length data:

plot(len ~ age, data = full_data,
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Total Length (mm)",
     main = "Creek Chub: Age vs Length",
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3))

Now, let’s fit the Von Bertalanffy model. We need starting values for the parameters. These are some good starting values based on published data.

sv_manual <- list(Linf = 200, K = 0.3, t0 = -1)

Now we define the Von Bertalanffy function and fit the model using nls() (nonlinear least squares):

library(minpack.lm)

vb <- vbFuns("Typical")
sv <- vbStarts(len ~ age, data = full_data)

fit <- nlsLM(len ~ vb(age, Linf, K, t0),
             data = full_data,
             start = sv)

summary(fit)

summary(fit)

Let’s extract the parameter estimates:

coef(fit)

Interpret each one in the context of Creek Chub biology:

The “Coaster” Brook Trout (Salvelinus fontinalis), a lake-dwelling stream-spawning form of Brook Trout, was largely extirpated from southern Lake Superior and the Whittlesey Creek watershed due to over-fishing and habitat degradation. title: 7  Size structure
text:
7.1 PSD
PSD stands for “Proportional Stock Density”. It essentially means the proportion of fish of stock size that are of quality size or greater. This is a common metric used in fisheries management to assess the health of a fish stock and to make informed decisions about fishing regulations and conservation efforts.
To calculate PSD, you would typically use the following formula: \[
PSD = \left( \frac{\text{Number of fish} \geq \text{quality size}}{\text{Number of fish} \geq \text{stock size}} \right) \times 100
\]
The length at which a fish is considered to be of “quality size” can vary depending on the species, and we use Gabelhouse lengths. Gabelhouse lengths, developed in 1984, are standardized, minimum total lengths (in mm or inches) used to categorize fish populations into stock, quality, preferred, memorable, and trophy sizes for assessing fish population structure. These categories provide precise, universal metrics for measuring fisheries
Generally, Gabelhouse length categories are as follows: - Stock Length: The minimum length at which fish are considered part of the population. 20-26% of trophy size - Quality Length: The minimum length at which fish are considered of good eating quality. 26-40% of trophy size - Preferred Length: The minimum length at which fish are considered to be of preferred size for anglers. 40-60% of trophy size - Memorable Length: The minimum length at which fish are considered to be of memorable size for anglers. 60-80% of trophy size - Trophy Length: The minimum length at which fish are considered to be of trophy size for anglers. 80% or more of the maximum size
The PSD metric is important for fisheries management because it helps to determine the size structure of the fish population. A high PSD indicates that a large proportion of the fish are of quality size or greater, which can be a sign of a healthy fish stock. Conversely, a low PSD may indicate that the fish population is dominated by smaller, less desirable fish, which can be a sign of overfishing or poor habitat conditions.
We can also estimate an RSD if we want to know the proportion of fish that are of memorable size or larger. For RSD we use the following formula:
\[
RSD\text{-}X = \left( \frac{\text{Number of fish} \geq \text{size category X}}{\text{Number of fish} \geq \text{stock size}} \right) \times 100
\]
Remember, these metrics use standardized length categories defined for each species (Stock, Quality, Preferred, Memorable, Trophy). Consult psdVal() in the FSA package.

8.3 2. Fitting the L-W Model to Data from FSAdata
We’ll use the FSAdata package for real fish data (install and load if needed):
We will work with bluegill data from the FSAdata package, which includes multiple lengths (mm) and weight (g) measurements.

data(BluegillLM) # Length (mm), Weight (g)

ggplot(BluegillLM, aes(x=sl, y=wght)) +
  geom_point(color="steelblue") +
  labs(title="Bluegill Length-Weight Data", x="Standard Length (mm)", y="Weight (g)")+
  theme_classic()


8.3.1 Transforming for Linear Model
The L-W relationship is non-linear, but can be linearized by log-transforming:
\[ \log(W) = \log(a) + b \log(L) \]
Fit linear model:

mod <- lm(log10(wght) ~ log10(sl), data=BluegillLM)
summary(mod)

Plot the linear relationship:

ggplot(BluegillLM, aes(x=log10(sl), y=log10(wght))) +
  geom_point(color="steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", color="darkred", se=FALSE) +
  labs(title="Log-Transformed L-W Relationship", x="log10(Standard Length)", y="log10(Weight)")+

text:
11.2 Introduction
Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR) is one of the most widely used methods in fisheries science for estimating the abundance of a population when it is impossible to count every individual directly. The basic idea is simple: you catch a sample of fish, mark them in some way (a fin clip, a tag, a dye), release them back into the water, and then come back later to catch another sample. The proportion of marked fish you recapture in that second sample gives you information about how large the population is.
Think of it this way: if you marked 100 fish and released them into a lake, and then your second sample of 100 fish contained 50 marked individuals, you’d guess the population was around 200. If only 10 were marked, you’d guess the population was around 1,000.

11.2.1 Assumptions of CMR
Like all models, CMR relies on some assumptions. For the estimates to be valid, we generally need:

The population is closed: no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration occur between the marking and recapture events.
All individuals have an equal probability of being captured (equal catchability): marked and unmarked fish are equally likely to be caught in the second sample.
Marks are not lost and do not fall off between sampling events.
Marks are correctly identified all marked fish are recognized as marked during the recapture event.
Indivials are not trap happy or shy This follows #2. Tagging a fish won’t increase or reduce the chances of the fish being captured again

Keep these assumptions in mind: you will come back to them later in this assignment!

11.3 Exercise 1: Chapman’s Modified Lincoln-Petersen Estimator (5 pts)
You have already seen the Lincoln-Petersen estimator in this course. As a reminder, we use a slightly modified version developed by Chapman that performs better with small sample sizes. The Chapman estimator is:
\[
\hat{N} = \frac{(M + 1)(C + 1)}{R + 1} - 1
\]
Where:

\(M\) = Number of individuals captured, marked, and released in the first sample
\(C\) = Total number of individuals captured in the second sample
\(R\) = Number of recaptured (marked) individuals in the second sample

Trust me on this one: this formula is more reliable than the classic Lincoln-Petersen for the kinds of sample sizes we typically deal with in fisheries. This is the equation you should use any time you are asked for a mark-recapture abundance estimate.

11.4 Exercise 2: Confidence Intervals for \(\hat{N}\) (5 pts)
A point estimate is great, but we always want to know how precise it is. Seber (1982) worked out the variance of the Chapman estimator, which we can use to build a confidence interval. The variance is:
\[
Var(\hat{N}) = \frac{(M + 1)(C + 1)(M - R)(C - R)}{(R + 1)^2(R + 2)}
\]
And the 95% confidence interval is calculated as:
\[
\hat{N} \pm 1.96 \sqrt{Var(\hat{N})}
\]
The following R code implements both the Chapman estimator and the 95% CI using the same data from Exercise 1. Run it and make sure you understand what each line is doing:

M <-   # Number marked in first sample
C <-   # Total captured in second sample
R <-   # Recaptured marked individuals

# Chapman estimator
N_hat <- ((M + 1) * (C + 1)) / (R + 1) - 1

# Variance
Var_N <- ((M + 1) * (C + 1) * (M - R) * (C - R)) / ((R + 1)^2 * (R + 2))

# 95% Confidence Interval
CI_lower <- N_hat - 1.96 * sqrt(Var_N)
CI_upper <- N_hat + 1.96 * sqrt(Var_N)

12.2 Basic Mortality Computations
There are three main ways we can estimate mortality: absolute interval, interval mortality rate, and instantaneous mortality rate.
The equation for the absolute mortality rate is:
\[
\frac{N_t - N_{t+1}}{\hat{I_t}}
\]
Where \(N_t\) is individuals at time t, \(N_{t+1}\) is individuals at time t+1. And \(\hat{I_t}\) is the interval length. However, we usually estimate rates. We can estimate the morality rate using the following:
\[
A=\frac{N_t - N_{t+1}}{N_t}
\]
And \(S\) (survival being): \(S=1-A\)
Because of the “non-linear”, exponential nature of fish mortality, we tend to use the instantaneous mortality rate. These table shows how to estimate the rates and transform interval to instantaneous rates:

Mortality rates. Symbols are as follows: (A) is interval mortality rate; (Z) is instantaneous mortality rate; (\(\mu\)) is interval fishing mortality; (\(\upsilon\)) is interval natural mortality, (F) is instantaneous fishing mortality rate; and (M) is natural instantaneous mortality rate.








Mortality rates
Total
Fishing
Natural




Interval
\[
A = 1-e^{-z} = \mu + \upsilon
\]
\[
\mu=\frac{FA}{Z} = \frac{\upsilon F}M
\]
\[
\upsilon=\frac{MA}{Z} = \frac{\mu M}F
\]


Instantaneous
\[
Z=-log(1-A) = F +M
\]
\[
F=\frac{\mu Z}{A} = \frac{\mu M}\upsilon
\]
\[
M=\frac{\upsilon Z}{A} = \frac{\upsilon F}\mu
\]









Remember! 🧠



We use the natural log! every equation with log in here is the natural log!


A cool thing about Z is we can easily estimate the mortality rate for shorter intervals. Imagine \(Z_{year}\) is 0.8, then \(Z_{month}\) is 0.8/12. Supper handy!

13.1 Estimating abundance from Mark-Recapture Data
This is similar tothe exercise we did in class on Tuesday. You will be tasked with estimating abundance using data from a Mark-Recapture study. You will be doing it all in R and you are expected to upload your R script.
We will be using a slightly modified formula than the one from Tuesday. If I ask for a Mark-Recapture abundance estimate during the exam, this is the equation you should use. This equation has been proven to better at estimating fish abundance, it is a modification of the traditional Lincoln-Peterson estimator and it uses the following formula:
\[
\hat{N} = \frac{(M+1)(C+1)}{R+1}-1
\]
where \(\hat{N}\) is the estimated population abundance, M is the number of marked individuals in the population (usually number of individuals caught during the first sampling event), C is the number of individuals captured during the second attempt and R is the number of recaptures (number of marked individuals captured during the second attempt.
Seber in 1982 also figured out how to estimate the variance of \(\hat{N}\). And it is using this equation:
\[
V(\hat{N}) = \frac{(M+1)(C+1)(M-R)(C-R)}{(R+1)^2 (R+2)}-1
\]
m<-49
c<-143
r<-23

N<-(((m+1)*(c+1))/(r+1))-1

v<-(((m+1)*(c+1)*(m-r)*(c-r))/ (((r+1)^2)*(r+2))         )-1
The math behind this specific variance is pretty complicated, but what you need to know is: “it helps us estimate the Confidence Intervals!”. After we estimate the variance, we can estimate the confidence interval using:
\[
\hat{N} \pm 1.96(\sqrt{V(\hat{N})} \ )
\]
This example was developed by Dr. Ogle and modified by me:
Young and Hayes (2001) described a study where Brown Trout (Salmo trutta) in several rivers were captured by experienced fly fishers, tagged at the base of the dorsal fin with a colored dart tag, and then observed by divers drifting through the sample area two days later. In the Ugly River, 49 trout were marked, 143 fish were observed by the divers, and 23 fish observed by the divers were tagged.

text:
14.3 The Recruitment Curves

14.3.1 What is a Recruitment Curve?
A recruitment curve (or stock-recruitment model) describes the relationship between the number of spawners (stock) and the number of offspring that survive to a specific life stage (recruits). These models are fundamental in fisheries science because they help us understand how fish populations replenish themselves and how much harvesting a population can sustain.


14.3.2 Beverton-Holt Model
The Beverton-Holt model assumes that recruitment increases with spawner abundance but eventually levels off at an asymptote. In other words, at very high spawner densities, adding more spawners does not increase recruitment because of density-dependent effects such as competition for food and habitat.
The equation is:
\[R = \frac{\alpha S}{1 + \beta S}\]
Where:

\(R\) = number of recruits
\(S\) = spawner abundance (stock)
\(\alpha\) = the maximum recruitment rate per spawner at low stock sizes (slope near the origin)
\(\beta\) = a parameter that controls how quickly recruitment approaches the asymptote

Key feature: Recruitment reaches a plateau — it never decreases, no matter how many spawners there are.


14.3.3 Ricker Model
The Ricker model also assumes density-dependent recruitment, but with an important difference: at very high spawner densities, recruitment actually decreases. This can happen because of cannibalism, disease, or intense competition among offspring.
The equation is:
\[R = \alpha S \cdot e^{-\beta S}\]
Where:

\(R\) = number of recruits
\(S\) = spawner abundance (stock)
\(\alpha\) = recruits per spawner at low stock sizes
\(\beta\) = the density-dependent parameter controlling the rate of decline at high stock sizes

Key feature: Recruitment peaks at an intermediate spawner abundance and then declines — forming a dome shape.


14.3.4 Visual Comparison
The figure below shows the general shape of both recruitment curves:



Recruitment curve shapes


The Beverton-Holt curve approaches an asymptote (flat line) while the Ricker curve rises and then falls at high spawner densities.

text:
14.4 Step-by-Step Guide to Fitting Recruitment Curves in R

14.4.1 Step 1: Load the Required Package
We will use the FSA package. Make sure it is installed:

install.packages("FSA")  # only run this once

Load the package:

library(FSA)



14.4.2 Step 2: Load Your Data
Your data should be a .csv file with columns for year, stock, and recruits. Load it using read.csv():

mydata <- read.csv("recruitment_data.csv")



14.4.3 Step 3: Explore the Data
Always explore your data before running any model:

head(mydata)
str(mydata)
summary(mydata)

You should check:

How many observations (rows) do you have?
Are the column names correct?
Are there any missing values (NA)?



14.4.4 Step 4: Plot the Raw Data
Before fitting any model, always plot your data:

plot(recruits ~ stock, data = mydata,
     pch = 19, col = "darkblue",
     xlab = "Stock (Spawner Abundance)",
     ylab = "Recruits",
     main = "Stock-Recruitment Data")

This scatter plot will give you an initial idea of whether the data looks like it follows a Beverton-Holt pattern (leveling off) or a Ricker pattern (dome-shaped).


14.4.5 Step 5: Log-Transform the Recruits
Because stock-recruitment relationships are non-linear, we log-transform the recruits to help with model fitting:

mydata$logR <- log(mydata$recruits)







Remember!



In R, log() is the natural logarithm (ln). This is the same as LN() in Excel.




14.4.6 Step 6: Find Starting Values
Non-linear models (like Beverton-Holt and Ricker) need good starting values for the parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The FSA package has a handy function for this:

14.4.6.1 Starting values for Beverton-Holt:

bh_starts <- srStarts(recruits ~ stock, data = mydata, type = "BevertonHolt", param = 1)
unlist(bh_starts)



14.4.6.2 Starting values for Ricker:

ri_starts <- srStarts(recruits ~ stock, data = mydata, type = "Ricker", param = 1)
unlist(ri_starts)







What are starting values?



When fitting a non-linear model, R needs an initial guess for the parameters. It then iteratively improves these guesses until it finds the combination that best fits the data. Good starting values help the algorithm converge (find a solution) faster and more reliably.





14.4.7 Step 7: Fit the Beverton-Holt Model
We define the model formula and fit it using nls() (non-linear least squares):

# Define the Beverton-Holt model on the log scale
bh_formula <- logR ~ log((a * stock) / (1 + b * stock))

# Fit the model
bh_fit <- nls(bh_formula, data = mydata, start = bh_starts)

# Look at the results
summary(bh_fit)

The summary() output will show you the estimated values of \(\alpha\) (a) and \(\beta\) (b), along with standard errors and p-values.


14.4.8 Step 8: Fit the Ricker Model

# Define the Ricker model on the log scale
ri_formula <- logR ~ log(a * stock * exp(-b * stock))

# Fit the model
ri_fit <- nls(ri_formula, data = mydata, start = ri_starts)

# Look at the results
summary(ri_fit)



14.4.9 Step 9: Fit the Density-Independent (Linear) Model
For comparison, it is useful to also fit a simple density-independent model where recruitment is proportional to stock size:
\[R = \alpha S\]

# Define the density-independent model
di_formula <- logR ~ log(a * stock)

# Use only the alpha starting value
di_starts <- bh_starts[1]

# Fit the model
di_fit <- nls(di_formula, data = mydata, start = di_starts)

# Look at the results
summary(di_fit)



14.4.10 Step 10: Compare Models with ANOVA
We can compare all three models using an ANOVA to determine if the more complex models (Beverton-Holt, Ricker) provide a significantly better fit than the simpler density-independent model:

anova(di_fit, bh_fit, ri_fit)







Interpreting the ANOVA




A low p-value (e.g., p < 0.05) for a more complex model suggests it fits significantly better than the simpler model.
If the p-value is not significant, the simpler model may be sufficient — adding extra parameters does not improve the fit enough to justify the added complexity.





14.4.11 Step 11: Plot the Fitted Curves
Finally, overlay the fitted recruitment curves on your scatter plot:

# Plot the raw data
plot(recruits ~ stock, data = mydata,
     pch = 19, col = "darkgray",
     xlab = "Stock (Spawner Abundance)",
     ylab = "Recruits",
     main = "Stock-Recruitment Models")

# Add the Beverton-Holt curve (red)
curve((coef(bh_fit)[1] * x) / (1 + coef(bh_fit)[2] * x),
      from = 0, to = max(mydata$stock) * 1.1,
      col = "red", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)

# Add the Ricker curve (blue)
curve(coef(ri_fit)[1] * x * exp(-coef(ri_fit)[2] * x),
      from = 0, to = max(mydata$stock) * 1.1,
      col = "blue", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)

# Add the density-independent curve (black)
curve(coef(di_fit)[1] * x,
      from = 0, to = max(mydata$stock) * 1.1,
      col = "black", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)

# Add a legend
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Beverton-Holt", "Ricker", "Density-Independent"),
       col = c("red", "blue", "black"),
       lwd = 2, cex = 0.8)

15.1.1 Fitting the Beverton Holt Model
We will now fit the Beverton-Hort model:
\[R=\frac{\alpha S}{(1+ \beta S)}\] This model assumes that recruitment is an asymptotic function of spawner abundance.






Q3



Describe each component of the Beverton-Holt equation, and try to describe what an asymptotic function of spawner abundance means.
You may use any source to look at a definition of an asymptotic function (ChatGPT, Google, etc). But USE YOUR OWN WORDS TO DESCRIBE IT.


We will use package FSA (Fisheries Stock Assessments package). This is the best package in R to run fisheries management analyses. It is the same package you used for assignment#2. Load the package.

15.1.1.1 How to fit a Beverton-Holt model?
In order to fit a Beverton-Holt model: \(R=\frac{\alpha S}{(1+ \beta S)}\) we need to find a good value for \(\alpha\) and a good value for \(\beta\). This is REALLY HARD. Essentially, you come up with a value for \(\alpha\) and a value for \(\beta\) run the model, and see how far the points are from the predicted points (points predicted by the model). Then, we give \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) some different values and see if this model fits better. We do this until we find the best solution. This is extremely time consuming, and you would spend months trying to find te combination of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) that works best. Luckily, there is a great solution for this.
The first step, is finding a good first guess of alpha and beta. This will help us save time and find a good solution in the end. Finding good values is very hard. But there is some good R code that can help us with this!
Use this code but replace both y and x. We have three variables: year, stock, and recruits. Think which one of them is the response variable (y) and which one is the explanatory variable (x). Once you figure this out you can replca both y and x. Do not continue until you have confirmation this is correct!

bh1s <- srStarts(y~x,data=LakeTroutGIS,type="BevertonHolt",param=1)
unlist(bh1s) 

This code finds good starting values. But this are still not the best values for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).






Q4



What are your starting alpha and beta values?





15.1.2 Finding the best values
The first step to find the best values is to transform the data. This is because this relationship:

is not linear. We need to slightly transform the equation, in order to more easily compare the predicted vs. the observed. We will change the values to:
\[logR = log (\frac{\alpha S}{1+\beta S})\]
Trust me on the need to do this. As you move forward in your career, you will find that a lot of data needs to be log-transformed (in this case log is the natural logarithm!)
Let’s obtain the natural log of the recruits (logR)

LakeTroutGIS$logR<-log(LakeTroutGIS$recruits)

Excel has a great tool to find the best values (we will use this tool pretty often in this course!)
Save this csv with:

write.csv(LakeTroutGIS,file="labfile1.csv",row.names=F)

and open this file in Excel (DO NOT CLOSE R).
In Excel, next to logR create a new column called predicted logR, and estimate it using your starting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) values. Remember we are using the natural log. Use ln(), Also, do not write the numbers in the formula, rather, write them in a cell, and refer to that cell later on. Name your alpha: “alpha B-H”, and your beta “beta-BH”. Use the following formula:
\[logR = log (\frac{\alpha S}{1+\beta S})\] Now, in a new column (sqdiff) estimate the squared difference of observed logR and predicted logR, and estimate the sum of this column.
We will use a new add-in called solver. Add this add-in to your excel (you did this for assignment 1, with the data analysis add-in)
Use solver, and obtain the best alpha and beta values, for the B-H model. After doing this, transform the predicted logR into predicted Recruits (EXP(predicted logR)). We want the predicted recruits instead of the predicted logRecruits. Don’t know how or why to use solver? Raise your hand!

b) In Excel plot the relation between Stock and recruits with points, and the predicted recruits with a line. IS this a good model?


Now, let’s do the same thing, but with the density independent model.
For this model, we will use: \[logR = log (\alpha S)\]
Remember log is natural log (LN in excel).
In a new cell in excel, write the original alpha value, and name it alphalinear.
Now: 1) Create a new column called logRlinearmodel. 2) In this column, estimate the predicted values using the equation. 3) Use solver to find the best solution. 4) Compare the sum of the squared differences.






Q6

Now, finally, backtransform you logRlinearmodel (use EXP). In your previous plot, add a line with the values for the linear model. In this plot, now you should have: points for the observed data, and lines for both models.






Q7



Explain the differences between both models. Which do you think is better?


Now we are going to do everything in R. We will run both models, and compare them using an ANOVA. Because things are faster in R, we will also run the Ricker model.
I will provide you with all the code. For each line that I provide, try to comment what you think that line of code does. You can add comments using # after the code

bh1 <- logR~log((a*stock)/(1+b*stock))
bh1nls <- nls(bh1,data=LakeTroutGIS,start=bh1s)

bh2 <- logR~log(a*stock*exp(-b*stock))
bh2nls <- nls(bh2,data=LakeTroutGIS,start=bh1s)
anova(bh0nls,bh1nls,bh2nls)

A.3 What You Must Decide
Your team is responsible for developing your own management goal, objectives, and actions. The scenario folders provide data and context, not answers. Specifically, your team must:

Propose a long-range management goal appropriate to the fishery and its stakeholders.
Diagnose problems and potentials based on your analysis of the data and your literature search.

A.4 Required Components of the Management Plan Expanded Outline
Your expanded outline must follow the eight steps of the management process listed below. Each step should be developed with enough detail that a reader can evaluate your plan without attending the oral presentation.

A.4.1 Step 1. Management Goal

State a long-range vision of the future based on the goal of your management.
Articulate a clear view of the future that anyone can understand.



A.4.2 Step 2. Analysis of Resourc
Add the ones that are possible: - Physical attributes, such as surface area, watershed area, littoral area, thermal stratification, and other key features. These may or may not be available in your data; you may need to do an online search. - Chemical attributes, such as alkalinity, hardness, dissolved oxygen, and pH. These may or may not be available in your data; you may need to do an online search. - Biological attributes, such as fish community, plant community, and non-native species. These may or may not be available in your data; you may need to do an online search. - Human attributes, such as angling pressure, angling regulations, land use in the watershed, and shoreline development. These may or may not be available in your data; you may need to do an online search.


A.4.3 Step 3. Diagnosis of Problems and Potentials

Diagnose relevant problems with the habitat, fish, or human users.
Identify the resource potential that might overcome each problem.



A.4.4 Step 4. Management Objectives and Actions

Set quantifiable objectives with dates for accomplishment for each.
Each objective should relate to a resource problem identified in the previous step.
Prescribe one or more management actions to achieve each objective.
Management actions related to fish, habitat, and people (for each objective) are more likely to succeed than management actions related only to fish, habitat, or people.



A.4.5 Step 5. Organization of People, Equipment, and Budgets

Describe needs for human effort (time = money).
Describe needs for equipment (purchases and operation = money).
Describe needs for funding (supplies and travel = money).



A.4.6 Step 6. Implementation Plan

Design implementation so that effects of each management action can be determined.
Prescribe a timeline for implementing the management plan.
Indicate when each management action will be implemented.



A.4.7 Step 7. Evaluation Plan

Describe how achievement of management objectives will be evaluated.
Describe interim evaluations that may be needed to evaluate progress.



A.4.8 Step 8. Maintenance Plan

Describe how the management plan will be maintained.
Describe how the management plan will be updated.

Elk Fork Creek historically supported a self-sustaining wild brown trout population, but recent electrofishing surveys show declining catch rates and reduced size structure. At the same time, continuous temperature and dissolved oxygen monitoring suggest that summer thermal stress may be increasing. Land use changes in the watershed, including timber harvest, road construction, and residential development, may be contributing to habitat degradation. Your team will analyze fish population data and environmental monitoring data to evaluate the status of the trout fishery and develop a management plan that integrates fish, habitat, and human dimensions.

Other species include sculpin, blacknose dace, creek chub, and white sucker. Benthic macroinvertebrate communities have not been formally assessed but are assumed to be sensitive to sedimentation and thermal changes. Trout spawning occurs in the fall, and recruitment success is thought to depend on gravel quality and winter base flows.

title: Appendix F — Scenario 05: Walleye Harvest and Creel Survey Management
text:
F.2 Main Task
Lake Sandhill is a large, wind-swept natural lake with a historically productive walleye fishery. Walleye are maintained through a combination of natural reproduction and periodic supplemental stocking. A comprehensive creel survey program has been in place since 2012, providing detailed information on angling effort, catch, harvest, and angler demographics. Recent creel data suggest that total walleye harvest has increased while catch rates of larger fish have declined. Your team will analyze the creel survey data alongside standardized gill net survey results to develop a management plan that balances harvest opportunity with population sustainability.
crumbs: F  Scenario 05: Walleye Harvest and Creel Survey Management

title: Appendix F — Scenario 05: Walleye Harvest and Creel Survey Management
text:
F.3 Biological Background
Walleye are the most sought-after species at Lake Sandhill. Yellow perch, white bass, and freshwater drum are also present and contribute to angler catch. Walleye natural reproduction occurs in rocky shoreline areas but is variable from year to year. Fingerling walleye have been stocked at irregular intervals (2014, 2016, 2019, 2022). Forage includes young-of-year yellow perch, shiners, and fathead minnows.

title: Appendix F — Scenario 05: Walleye Harvest and Creel Survey Management
text:

Walleye fishing generates significant economic activity for the surrounding rural community.
Current regulations include a 15-inch minimum length limit and a 4-fish daily bag limit for walleye.
A special regulation (protected slot of 17 to 22 inches) was discussed but not implemented.
Ice fishing accounts for a substantial portion of annual walleye harvest.
Lakeshore cabin owners and a resort association are vocal stakeholders.
Water levels have fluctuated due to drought and wet cycles, affecting spawning habitat availability.

title: Appendix G — Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake
text:
G.2 Main Task
Mirror Lake is a small, moderately productive natural lake that has experienced two major stressors in recent years: the establishment of an invasive common carp population and a trend of declining water quality linked to nutrient loading from surrounding residential and agricultural land use. Agency biologists have been monitoring the fish community, water quality, and aquatic vegetation since 2010. Your team will analyze these datasets to assess how invasive carp and nutrient enrichment are affecting the fishery and develop a management plan that addresses both stressors while maintaining recreational fishing opportunities.
crumbs: G  Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake

title: Appendix G — Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake
text:
G.3 Biological Background
The native fish community includes bluegill, largemouth bass, channel catfish, and yellow bullhead. Common carp were first detected in 2013 and have become increasingly abundant. Carp are believed to be degrading water quality through bioturbation (stirring up bottom sediments) and uprooting submerged aquatic vegetation. Aquatic vegetation coverage has declined from approximately 40% of the littoral zone in 2010 to less than 15% in recent surveys. Algal blooms have become more frequent.
crumbs: G  Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake

title: Appendix G — Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake
text:
G.4 Management Context

Mirror Lake is a popular fishing destination for families and beginning anglers.
A lakeside community association of approximately 120 homeowners is concerned about water quality, property values, and the aesthetic condition of the lake.
Current fishing regulations are standard statewide limits.
The county soil and water conservation district has offered technical assistance for nutrient management plans on adjacent farmland.
A commercial carp removal operator has been consulted but costs are substantial.
State invasive species funding may be available through a competitive grant program.

title: Appendix G — Scenario 06: Invasive Species and Water Quality in a Small Lake
text:

title: Appendix H — Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery
text:
H.2 Main Task
Millstone Reservoir is a flood-control impoundment located on the edge of a growing metropolitan area. The reservoir supports a mixed warmwater fishery with largemouth bass, channel catfish, white crappie, and hybrid striped bass (stocked). As the surrounding urban area expands, the reservoir faces increasing pressure from both anglers and non-angling users (kayakers, swimmers, shoreline picnickers). Stormwater runoff has increased nutrient and sediment inputs, and periodic fish kills have been reported during late summer. Your team will analyze fish population, environmental, and user survey data to develop a management plan that sustains the fishery while addressing urban growth pressures.
crumbs: H  Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery

title: Appendix H — Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery
text:
H.3 Biological Background
Largemouth bass and channel catfish are naturally reproducing. White crappie recruitment is highly variable. Hybrid striped bass are stocked every other year to diversify angling opportunities but do not reproduce. Gizzard shad are the dominant forage species and periodically experience large die-offs during cold winters. Blue-green algae blooms occur during July and August in most years, occasionally prompting swimming advisories. Threadfin shad were stocked in the early 2000s but have not persisted after severe winters.
crumbs: H  Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery

title: Appendix H — Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery
text:
H.4 Management Context

The reservoir is managed jointly by the city parks department and the state wildlife agency.
Angling is the second most popular recreational activity after trail use.
A local bass club, a catfish anglers association, and a kayak club have all expressed opinions about management priorities.
Urban stormwater management is handled by the city, and coordination has been limited.
A fish consumption advisory for mercury is in effect for largemouth bass longer than 15 inches.
Bank fishing access is limited; two boat ramps are available but crowded on weekends.
The city has allocated a modest annual budget for fisheries enhancement.
crumbs: H  Scenario 07: Urban Reservoir Mixed Warmwater Fishery

text:

Your team must propose a long-range management goal that balances fishery quality, urban development pressures, multiple user groups, and environmental constraints at Millstone Reservoir.

reservoir_environment.csv: Monthly environmental monitoring data (May through October, 2012 to 2025) including dissolved oxygen profiles, Secchi depth, surface temperature, and algal bloom indicators.
user_survey.csv: Biennial user intercept survey data (2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024) covering user type, activity, satisfaction, and management priorities.

Summarize user demographics, satisfaction trends, and stated management priorities.
Assess whether hybrid striped bass stocking is contributing to angler catch and satisfaction.
Identify conflicts between user groups and potential management solutions.
Review published literature on urban reservoir fisheries management.
